questions.q: What are sticky ends in DNA?
options: Single stranded portions at the ends of the DNA

questions.solution: Restriction enzymes cut the strand of DNA a little away from the center of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This leaves single stranded portions at the ends. There are overhanging stretches called sticky ends on each strand. These are named so because they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase. Replicating independently of the control of chromosomal DNA
Replicating with control of chromosomal DNA
questions.solution: You know that plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA. Some plasmids may have only one or two copies per cell whereas others may have >15-100 copies per cell. Their numbers can go even higher. If we are able to link an alien piece of DNA with bacteriophage or plasmid DNA, we can multiply its numbers equal to the copy number of the plasmid or bacteriophage. Vectors used at present, are engineered in such a way that they help easy linking of foreign DNA and selection of recombinants from non-recombinants

questions.q: What type of pathogen can deliver genes to transform normal plant cells?
questions.solution: You may be surprised to know that we have learnt the lesson of transferring genes into plants and animals from bacteria and viruses which have known this for ages – how to deliver genes to transform eukaryotic cells and force them to do what the bacteria or viruses want. For example, Agrobacterium tumifaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as ‘T-DNA’ to transform normal plant cells into a tumor and direct these tumor cells to produce the chemicals required by the pathogen. Similarly, retroviruses in animals have the ability to transform normal cells into cancerous cells. A better understanding of the art of delivering genes by pathogens in their eukaryotic hosts has generated knowledge to transform these tools of pathogens into useful vectors for delivering genes of interest to humans. The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumifaciens has now been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants

questions.q: What is the main reason for DNA being unable to pass through cell membranes?
options: cannot enter the bacterium through pores in its cell wall
questions.solution: Since DNA is a hydrophilic molecule, it cannot pass through cell membranes. Why? In order to force bacteria to take up the plasmid, the bacterial cells must first be made ‘competent’ to take up DNA. This is done by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation, such as calcium, which increases the efficiency with which DNA enters the bacterium through pores in its cell wall. Recombinant DNA can then be forced into such cells by incubating the cells with recombinant DNA on ice, followed by placing them briefly at 420C (heat shock), and then putting them back on ice. This enables the bacteria to take up the recombinant DNA.

questions.q: What does PCR stand for?
questions.solution: PCR stands for Polymerase Chain Reaction. In this reaction, multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest is synthesised in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides that are complementary to the regions of DNA) and the enzyme DNA polymerase. The enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template. If the process of replication of DNA is repeated many times, the segment of DNA can be amplified to approximately billion times, i.e., 1 billion copies are made. Such repeated amplification is achieved by the use of a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus), which remain active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double stranded DNA. The amplified fragment if desired can now be used to ligate with a vector for further cloning >Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) : Each cycle has three steps: (i) Denaturation; >(ii) Primer annealing; and (iii) Extension of primers >.

questions.solution: Each restriction endonuclease functions by ‘inspecting’ the length of a DNA sequence. Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it will bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar -phosphate backbones. Each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequences in the DNA.

Similarly, retroviruses in animals have the ability to transform normal cells into cancerous cells. A better understanding of the art of delivering genes by pathogens in their eukaryotic hosts has generated knowledge to transform these tools of pathogens into useful vectors for delivering genes of interest to humans. The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumifaciens has now been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants. A. Treatment with Protease1. Removes proteins
B. Addition of Chilled Ethanol2. Precipitates DNA
C. Removal of RNA3. Releases DNA from cells
D. Isolation of Macromolecules4. Removes RNA
questions.solution: Protease removes proteins, chilled ethanol precipitates DNA, ribonuclease removes RNA, and isolation of macromolecules releases DNA from cells.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Techniques in Recombinant DNA TechnologyDescription
A. Restriction Enzyme Digestion1. Visualizes DNA fragments
B. Agarose Gel Electrophoresis2. Cuts DNA at specific sites
C. Ligation3. Joins DNA fragments
D. PCR4. DNA segments
questions.solution: Restriction enzyme digestion cuts DNA at specific sites, agarose gel electrophoresis is used to visualize DNA fragments, ligation joins DNA fragments, and PCR amplifies DNA segments.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Components of PCRFunction
A. Primers1. Provides building blocks for DNA synthesis
B. DNA Polymerase2. Extends the primers
C. Nucleotides3. Short sequences that initiate DNA synthesis
D. Template DNA4. The DNA to be amplified
questions.solution: Primers are short sequences that initiate DNA synthesis, DNA polymerase extends the primers, nucleotides are the building blocks for DNA synthesis, and template DNA is the DNA to be amplified.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Bioreactor ComponentsFunction
A. Agitator System1. Ensures even mixing of contents
B. Oxygen Delivery System2. Maintains appropriate temperature
C. Foam Control System3. Prevents foam formation
D. Temperature Control System4. Supplies oxygen to the culture
questions.solution: The agitator system ensures even mixing, the oxygen delivery system supplies oxygen to the culture, the foam control system prevents foam formation, and the temperature control system maintains the appropriate temperature.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Downstream ProcessingActivities
A. Purification1. Ensures product meets standards
B. Separation2. Isolates the product from other components
C. Formulation3. Prepares the product for market
D. Quality Control4. Removes impurities
questions.solution: Purification removes impurities, separation isolates the product, formulation prepares the product for market, and quality control ensures the product meets standards.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Types of BioreactorsDescription
A. Stirred-Tank Reactor1. Gas is bubbled through liquid medium
B. Airlift Reactor2. Contains immobilized cells or enzymes
C. Bubble Column Reactor3. Uses an internal or external loop for circulation
D. Packed Bed Reactor4. Has a stirrer for mixing contents
questions.solution: A stirred-tank reactor has a stirrer for mixing contents, an airlift reactor uses an internal or external loop for circulation, a bubble column reactor bubbles gas through the liquid medium, and a packed bed reactor contains immobilized cells or enzymes.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q:
Bioreactor ConditionsPurpose
A. Temperature Control1. Maintains the appropriate acidity or alkalinity
B. pH Control2. Prevents overheating or undercooling
C. Oxygen Delivery3. Ensures cells have sufficient oxygen
D. Foam Control4. Prevents excessive foam formation
questions.solution: Temperature control prevents overheating or undercooling, pH control maintains appropriate acidity or alkalinity, oxygen delivery ensures cells have sufficient oxygen, and foam control prevents excessive foam formation.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q: A DNA sequence in a genome where replication is initiated is called ___
questions.solution: A DNA sequence in a genome where replication is initiated is called origin of replication

questions.q: The large vessels that are used for the large-scale production of biotechnological products from raw resources is called ___
questions.solution: The large vessels that are used for the large-scale production of biotechnological products from raw resources are called Bioreactors.

questions.q: The method of separating and purifying foreign gene products once the biosynthetic stage is completed is called ___
questions.solution: The method of separating and purifying foreign gene products once the biosynthetic stage is completed is called downstream processing

questions.q: ____ is a full form of PCR.
questions.solution: The fullform of PCR is polymerase chain reaction

questions.q: The molecular scissors used to cut DNA sequences from a particular site is called __.
questions.solution: The molecular scissors used to cut DNA sequences from a particular site is called restriction enzyme.

questions.q: This enzyme used for the degradation of chitin, which forms the main component of the cell wall of fungi is the function of ___.
questions.solution: This enzyme used for the degradation of chitin, which forms the main component of the cell wall of fungi is the function of Chitinase

questions.q: What is the difference between Plasmid DNA and Chromosomal DNA?
options: Plasmid DNA is an extra Chromosomal DNA molecule found in bacteria while chromosomal DNA forms the complete DNA of an entity found inside the chromosomes
The plasmid DNA is found in plants while the chromosomal DNA is found in animals
The plasmid DNA is smaller while the chromosomal DNA is larger
questions.solution: The difference between Plasmid DNA and Chromosomal DNA is Plasmid DNA is an extra Chromosomal DNA molecule found in bacteria while chromosomal DNA forms the complete DNA of an entity found inside the chromosomes
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q: What is the difference between RNA and DNA?
options: RNA is single stranded while DNA is double stranded
RNA is stable while DNA is unstable
RNA is found in most of the organisms as genetic material while DNA is rare
questions.solution: The difference between DNA and RNA is that RNA is single stranded while DNA is double stranded

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes catalyse the removal of nucleotides from the ends of DNA?
questions.solution: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA

questions.q: Which of the given statements is correct in the context of visualizing DNA molecules separated by agarose gel electrophoresis?
options: DNA can be seen in visible light
DNA can be seen without staining in visible light
Ethidium bromide-stained DNA can be seen in visible light
Ethidium bromide-stained DNA can be seen under exposure to  UV light
questions.solution: The separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q: ‘Restriction’ in Restriction enzyme refers to:
options: Cleaving of the phosphodiester bond in DNA by the enzyme
Cutting of DNA at a specific position only
Prevention of the multiplication of bacteriophage by the host bacteria
questions.solution: Each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequences in the DNA.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q: Which of the following is not required in the preparation of a recombinant  DNA molecule?
questions.solution: Only molecular enzymes are needed for the preparation of a recombinant DNA molecule.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA molecules are separated on the basis  of their:
questions.solution: In agarose gel electrophoresis, DNA molecules are separated on the basis of their charge, size and charge to size ratio.
questions.subject: Zoology

questions.q: The most important feature of a plasmid to serve as a vector in gene cloning experiment is:
options: Presence of sites for restriction endonuclease
questions.solution: Origin of replication (ori) is a sequence from where replication starts and any piece of DNA when linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells.

questions.q: While isolating DNA from bacteria, which of the following enzymes is not  required?
questions.solution: Deoxyribonuclease will denature the isolated DNA.

questions.q: Which of the following contributed in popularising the PCR (polymerase  chain reactions) technique?
questions.solution: Availability of ‘Thermostable’ DNA polymerase contributed in popularising the PCR (polymerase chain reactions) technique.

questions.q: An antibiotic resistance gene in a vector usually helps in the selection of:
questions.solution: An antibiotic resistance gene in a vector usually helps in the selection of transformed cells as they cells do not die in the presence of the antibiotic.

questions.q: Significance of the ‘heat shock’ method in bacterial transformation is to facilitate:
options: Binding of DNA to the cell wall
Uptake of DNA through membrane transport proteins
Uptake of DNA through transient pores in the bacterial cell wall
questions.solution: Heat shock enables the bacteria to take up the recombinant DNA.

questions.q: The role of DNA ligase in the construction of a recombinant DNA  molecule is:
options: Formation of a phosphodiester bond between two DNA fragments
Formation of hydrogen bonds between sticky ends of DNA  fragments
Ligation of all purine and pyrimidine bases
questions.solution: When cut by the same restriction enzyme, the resultant DNA fragments have the same kind of ‘sticky-ends’ and, these can be joined together (end-to-end) using DNA ligases.

questions.q: Which of the following bacteria is not a source of restriction endonuclease?
questions.solution: Entamoeba coli does not produce any restriction endonuclease.

questions.q: Which of the following steps are catalysed by Taq DNA polymerase in a PCR reaction?
options: Annealing of primers to template DNA
Extension of primer end on the template DNA
questions.solution: The enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template.

questions.q: Which of the following should be chosen for the best yield if one were to produce a recombinant protein in large amounts?
options: A stirred-tank bioreactor without in-lets and out-lets
questions.solution: Continuous type of culturing method produces a larger biomass leading to higher yields of desired protein.

options: It recognises a palindromic nucleotide sequence
It can produce the same kind of sticky ends in different DNA  molecules
questions.solution: Restriction enzymes are mainly isolated from bacterias.

options: Sequence in which the restriction enzyme is isolated

questions.q: Competent cells have the ability to :
options: Take up dna from the surroundings through cell wall
questions.solution: Competent cell refers to the capability of the cell wall of bacteria to uptake hydrophilic DNA fragments when treated with divalent ions through the cell membrane.

questions.solution: Proteases are the enzymes which digest the protein present inside the cell. Proteases ensure the isolation of DNA without its contamination with proteins.

questions.q: Endonucleases cut at :
questions.solution: Restriction endonucleases will bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar -phosphate backbones.

questions.solution: DNA is made visible by staining it with Ethidium bromide, which on exposure to UV rays, appears to be orange-coloured bands.

questions.q: Calcium chloride helps in:
options: Formation of pores on cell wall
questions.solution: When Ca2+ ions are rubbed against the cell wall, it results in the enlargement of the diameter of the pores and allows the uptake of foreign DNA fragments.
